title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (sliding window + HashSet).
shortTitle: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters — Sliding Window + HashSet

s1_definition.profdef: This problem finds the length of the longest contiguous substring that contains no repeated character. The sliding-window solution maintains a window of unique characters using a set or a last-seen index map, expanding the right edge to include new characters and contracting the left edge whenever a duplicate appears, tracking the maximum window size. It runs in linear time, since each character enters and leaves the window at most once.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India scans a stream of single-character operation codes and wants the longest run with no repeated code, as a measure of the longest stretch of distinct operations. Imagine a stretchy window over the codes. You push the right edge forward to grab new codes as long as they are all different. The instant a code repeats inside the window, you pull the left edge forward past the earlier copy, so the window again holds only distinct codes, and you remember the widest window seen.
s1_definition.oneliner: Grow the window on the right, shrink it from the left past any duplicate, and track the widest all-unique window.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem finds the length of the longest contiguous substring that contains no repeated character. The sliding-window solution maintains a window of unique characters using a set or a last-seen index map, expanding the right edge to include new characters and contracting the left edge whenever a duplicate appears, tracking the maximum window size. It runs in linear time, since each character enters and leaves the window at most once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India scans a stream of single-character operation codes and wants the longest run with no repeated code, as a measure of the longest stretch of distinct operations. Imagine a stretchy window over the codes. You push the right edge forward to grab new codes as long as they are all different. The instant a code repeats inside the window, you pull the left edge forward past the earlier copy, so the window again holds only distinct codes, and you remember the widest window seen.

**One line to remember:** Grow the window on the right, shrink it from the left past any duplicate, and track the widest all-unique window.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute force checks every substring for uniqueness, which is cubic or quadratic. The sliding window gets linear time by never re-examining characters unnecessarily. You keep a window defined by a left and a right index, and a structure that records which characters are currently inside the window.

Using a HashSet, you move the right index forward one character at a time. Before adding the character at the right, you check whether it is already in the set. If it is, you remove characters from the left end of the window, advancing the left index and removing each character from the set, until the duplicate is gone. Then you add the new character and update the maximum length as the current window width, right minus left plus one. This guarantees the window always holds only distinct characters.

A faster variant replaces the set with a map from character to its last-seen index. When you encounter a character already seen and whose last-seen index is at or after the current left, you jump the left index directly to one past that last-seen index, instead of removing characters one by one. This still runs in linear time but does fewer operations because the left edge leaps forward in one step rather than crawling.

A senior point is why the total work is linear despite the inner contraction. The left index only ever moves forward, never backward, across the whole scan, and the right index also only moves forward. So each index traverses the string at most once, giving linear time overall even though a single step may contract the window by several characters. Articulating this amortized argument is what interviewers want, because the nested-looking loop can appear quadratic at a glance.

Another senior point is the alphabet and the max update placement. With the set approach you update the maximum after ensuring the window is valid; with the last-seen-index approach you must guard that the remembered index is within the current window before jumping, otherwise an old index outside the window would wrongly shrink it. For an open character set a HashMap is right; for a fixed small alphabet a plain array indexed by character is faster.

A small finance-domain example: `Set<Character> win=new HashSet<>(); int l=0,best=0; for(int r=0;r<s.length();r++){ while(win.contains(s.charAt(r))) win.remove(s.charAt(l++)); win.add(s.charAt(r)); best=Math.max(best,r-l+1); }` finds the longest distinct run.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India logs a compact string of single-character operation codes for a session and wants the longest contiguous run with no repeated code, as a signal of the longest stretch of distinct operations before any repeat. The log can be long, so the scan must be linear. Finding the longest substring without repeating characters by sliding window is exactly this.

This is exactly how the sliding window works in Java — expanding the right edge for new codes and contracting the left edge past any duplicate so the window stays all-unique.

Problem 2 — Some sessions repeat a code immediately, giving a best run of one, and the empty log gives zero, and both must be handled cleanly. This shows the immediate-repeat and empty-input edge cases, plus the amortized-linear reasoning.

What the code will do: a `DistinctRunFinder` with `longestDistinctRun(String codes)` using a HashSet sliding window that tracks the widest all-unique window. The demo finds the longest distinct run in operation-code strings.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the operation-code string `abcabcbb`.

Step 1: left is zero, the window set is empty, best is zero. Right moves to `a` at index zero; `a` is not in the set, so we add it, the window is `a`, width one, best becomes one.

Step 2: right moves to `b` at index one; not in the set, add it, window `a b`, width two, best becomes two. Right moves to `c` at index two; not in the set, add it, window `a b c`, width three, best becomes three.

Step 3: right moves to `a` at index three; `a` is already in the set, so we shrink from the left: remove `a` at index zero and advance left to one. Now `a` is gone, so we add the new `a`, window `b c a`, width three, best stays three.

Step 4: right moves to `b` at index four; `b` is in the set, so remove `b` at index one, advance left to two, add `b`, window `c a b`, width three. The same pattern continues for the next `c`.

Step 5: right moves to `b` at index six; `b` is in the set, shrink removing from the left until `b` is gone, then add. The final `b` at index seven likewise forces a shrink. Throughout, the best width observed is three, the length of `abc`, so the method returns three. For `bbbbb` every new `b` forces an immediate shrink to a single character, so the best is one, and for `pwwkew` the best distinct run is `wke` with length three.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T21:00:00Z INFO Longest distinct run = 3
2026-10-26T21:00:00Z INFO Run = 3
2026-10-26T21:00:00Z INFO Longest distinct run = 1
2026-10-26T21:00:00Z INFO Run = 1
2026-10-26T21:00:00Z INFO Longest distinct run = 3
2026-10-26T21:00:00Z INFO Run = 3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: "abcabcbb"  left=0 window={} best=0
    │
    ▼
  for right: if c in window, shrink left until gone; add c; best=max(best,width)
    │ a,b,c → window{a,b,c} best=3
    │ a dup → remove a, left=1, add a → {b,c,a} width 3
    │ b dup → remove b, left=2 ... stays width 3
    ▼
  best = 3  ("abc")
    ▼
  Output: longest distinct-code run length
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters asks for the length of the longest contiguous run with no repeated character, and I solve it with a sliding window in linear time. I keep a window defined by a left and right index and a set of the characters currently inside. I move the right edge forward to include new characters, and whenever the incoming character is already in the window, I advance the left edge, removing characters, until the duplicate is gone, then add the new character and update the maximum window width.

The variant I usually prefer replaces the set with a map from each character to its last-seen index, so instead of crawling the left edge one step at a time past a duplicate, I jump it directly to one past the duplicate's last position, which does fewer operations while staying linear. With that variant I must guard that the remembered index lies within the current window before jumping, otherwise a stale index outside the window would wrongly shrink it.

The point interviewers want is why this is linear despite the inner contraction loop. Both the left and right indices only ever move forward across the whole string and never backward, so each traverses the input at most once, giving amortized linear time even though a single step may collapse the window by several characters. I also handle the edges: an immediate repeat yields a best run of one and an empty input yields zero.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on compact session logs of single-character operation codes to find the longest stretch of distinct operations before any code repeated, running linearly over long logs. Explaining the expand-and-contract window, the last-seen-index optimization with its in-window guard, and the amortized-linear argument shows the interviewer that I understand the sliding window as a general technique, not just this one problem.
